case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Communications Act’s FCC monetary forfeiture scheme—allowing the FCC to determine and announce large civil penalties through administrative orders before any jury trial—violates the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right and Article III by functionally adjudicating traditional legal claims outside an Article III court.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VII (jury trial in “Suits at common law”) and Article III (judicial power vested in Article III courts), as applied to the Communications Act provisions governing FCC assessment/imposition and judicial enforcement (“recovery”) of monetary forfeitures (including provisions described in argument as requiring de novo judicial proceedings for recovery).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The federal parties (FCC/United States) argue that the FCC’s forfeiture instruments (e.g., notices/orders stating what the carrier ‘owes’) are not constitutionally problematic because they are non-binding and do not finally compel payment; instead, any actual collection of money must occur in an Article III court where the defendant can obtain a de novo proceeding (and, if the Seventh Amendment applies, a jury). On this view, the agency’s action is closer to a charging document (like an indictment/complaint) that authorizes litigation rather than a final adjudication, and because the FCC’s determination has no preclusive effect in later court litigation, the Seventh Amendment/Article III concerns identified in SEC v. Jarkesy are not triggered at the agency stage. The government leans on older precedent (e.g., Meeker and Hof) to support the constitutionality of administrative, nonfinal/nonbinding determinations that precede a full judicial trial.
case_analysis.respondent_position: AT&T and Verizon contend that under SEC v. Jarkesy, the Seventh Amendment protects the right to a jury trial when the government seeks civil penalties that replicate traditional common-law actions; Congress cannot evade that guarantee by routing penalty determinations through an agency. They argue the FCC’s scheme is functionally an adjudication of liability and penalty amount—an ‘imposition’ in substance—even if the target can refuse to pay and force the government to sue to collect. In their view, allowing the FCC to ‘assess’ penalties via an agency process (especially where the agency’s order is designed to coerce compliance and has significant practical consequences) is precisely the kind of administrative penalty adjudication Jarkesy condemned; the possibility of later judicial collection litigation does not cure the constitutional defect because many penalty regimes similarly require a later collection step. They also suggest that, at minimum, if the Court accepts the government’s “nonbinding” characterization, the agency’s forfeiture order must carry no legal weight beyond ‘paper’—no binding effect, no coercive leverage grounded in adjudicative authority, and potentially restitution/return of funds if monies were paid under the unconstitutional scheme.
key_precedents: Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Comm’n, 430 U.S. 442 (1977)
Hof (as referenced in oral argument; cited by the government for the proposition that nonbinding administrative determinations do not trigger Seventh Amendment concerns)
Meeker (as referenced in oral argument; relied on by the government to argue nonbinding administrative steps are permissible)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to emphasize the practical coercion of an FCC forfeiture order, and I do not discount that regulated parties may feel intense pressure to pay. But under our precedents (as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan stress), the constitutional line has turned on binding legal effect: § 504’s express “trial de novo” in any “suit for the recovery” means the FCC order must “cut off no defense” and take no fact issue from the Article III court or jury, placing this within Meeker/Hof rather than Jarkesy, where the agency itself finally fixed liability and imposed penalties with legal force. The best minimalist course is to decide on that statutory ground and make explicit that the forfeiture order carries no preclusive effect and commands no deference in court; concerns about real-world leverage cannot justify a broader Article III/Seventh Amendment ruling when Congress has preserved de novo judicial adjudication. On my methodology, the respondents’ coercion argument sounds in policy and practical burdens, but it does not overcome the statute’s structural guarantee that only a court judgment can compel payment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make a serious point that an FCC forfeiture order can be practically coercive, but under an original public meaning approach the constitutional line is whether the Executive may conclusively determine liability and compel payment without an Article III judgment and (where applicable) a jury. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 504’s command that any “suit for the recovery” “shall be a trial de novo” means the FCC’s order must “cut off no defense” and cannot bind court or jury—bringing this within Meeker/Hof’s permissible model of nonpreclusive administrative preliminaries. Jarkesy is therefore distinguishable because the agency there finally adjudicated and imposed penalties with legal effect, while here the only legally operative adjudication occurs in court; practical leverage alone cannot convert a nonbinding assessment into an exercise of the judicial Power. I would, however, insist our disposition make explicit that “de novo” entails no deference and no preclusion, addressing the coercion concern to the extent it could otherwise creep in through practice.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to emphasize the real-world pressure an FCC forfeiture order can exert, but that practical leverage is not the same as binding legal consequence for Article III/Seventh Amendment purposes. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, the Communications Act channels any “suit for the recovery” into a mandatory “trial de novo,” which under Meeker’s logic means the administrative order must “cut off no defense” and take no fact question from the court or jury; on that understanding, the order functions like a nonbinding accusation rather than a final punitive judgment. Jarkesy is therefore distinguishable because it involved an agency adjudication that itself finally fixed penalty liability with legal force, whereas here payment cannot be compelled and liability cannot be conclusively determined until an Article III court enters judgment after fresh adjudication. If coercion is the worry, the proper judicial move is to enforce the statute’s de novo guarantee strictly—no preclusion, no deference, no evidentiary shortcut—not to constitutionalize the preliminary administrative step into an Article III violation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that § 504’s “trial de novo” can be read, Meeker-style, to ensure the FCC order “cuts off no defense” and has no preclusive effect, thereby preserving an Article III court (and potentially a jury) as the only body that can enter a money judgment. But that statutory safeguard does not answer the constitutional problem Jarkesy identifies: Congress has still assigned the government’s initial adjudication of punitive liability and a specific penalty amount to the Executive, and the practical operation of that order predictably coerces settlement and compliance long before any de novo suit is filed. Meeker and Hof involved genuinely advisory/noncoercive preliminaries; here the agency’s public determination of guilt and dollars is the operative event for many regulated parties, making the jury right contingent on the target’s willingness to resist and the government’s decision to sue. Under my pragmatic approach focused on real-world effects and access to justice, a “paper” de novo opportunity later cannot cure an up-front administrative penalty determination that functions, in practice, as punishment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the best objection: even if formally nonpreclusive, an FCC forfeiture order can be practically coercive and may function like an agency penalty adjudication in substance. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the statutory line Congress drew is at the “suit for the recovery” and it expressly requires a “trial de novo,” which is most coherently read to mean the FCC order cannot bind the court on liability or amount—tracking Meeker’s premise that the administrative step must “cut off no defense” and “take no question of fact” from court or jury. On my pragmatic textualist approach, that reading both fits the Communications Act’s structure and avoids extending Jarkesy to invalidate a scheme where the first legally operative adjudication and enforceable money judgment occur only in Article III. The appropriate way to address the coercion concern is to enforce the de novo/no-preclusion rule strictly (no deference, no issue preclusion, no evidentiary shortcut), not to recharacterize a non-self-executing order as constitutionally final.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor offer the best counter: that an FCC forfeiture order is practically coercive and so functions like the sort of agency penalty adjudication Jarkesy condemns. But under my textualist/originalist approach, the constitutional hinge is where binding legal consequences attach, and the Communications Act’s “suit for the recovery” plus mandatory “trial de novo” (as the Chief Justice stresses) means the FCC’s order cannot itself compel payment, cannot fix liability with legal force, and—critically—must “cut off no defense” in court under Meeker. If we make explicit in our disposition (and expect lower courts to enforce) that the order has no preclusive effect, no deference, and no evidentiary shortcut that displaces the jury’s role, then Jarkesy is distinguishable because there the agency itself entered a final, binding penalty judgment. I therefore remain with Petitioner, while insisting the opinion police the de novo requirement so the government cannot convert practical leverage into legal compulsion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the most serious point: the FCC’s announced forfeiture can be practically coercive and may, as a matter of real-world leverage, resemble an agency-imposed penalty. But under the statutory structure Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—and consistent with Meeker’s “cuts off no defense” principle—the constitutionally operative event is the Article III “suit for the recovery” that “shall be a trial de novo,” where the FCC order must have no preclusive effect and no binding legal consequence as to liability or amount. Jarkesy is therefore distinguishable because the agency proceeding there itself finally fixed liability and imposed penalties with legal force, whereas here the agency step is antecedent and noncompulsive in law, provided we make explicit (as Justice Gorsuch urges) that de novo means no deference/no preclusion. The coercion concern is meaningful as a policy matter, but absent legal compulsion or foreclosure of defenses, it does not supply a Seventh Amendment or Article III violation under our history-and-precedent framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor are right to press that an FCC forfeiture order may be practically coercive, but under a textualist and original-public-meaning approach the constitutional trigger is legal effect: whether the agency determination itself binds, compels payment, or precludes defenses. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 504’s command that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed … shall be a trial de novo” is best read to mean exactly what Meeker required—an administrative step that “cuts off no defense” and “takes no question of fact from either court or jury,” with no deference or preclusion in court. Jarkesy is distinguishable on that ground because the agency there finally adjudicated and imposed a penalty with binding legal force; here, the only legally operative adjudication is the Article III de novo action where the Seventh Amendment jury right (if applicable) is preserved. If “coercion” is the concern, the appropriate judicial move is to enforce de novo rigorously—foreclosing any judicial reliance on the FCC’s findings—rather than recharacterizing a nonbinding precursor as an unconstitutional penalty adjudication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Meeker-based avoidance framing is the best petitioner point, but it assumes away the constitutional harm Jarkesy identifies: Congress may not assign the government’s initial adjudication of liability and a punitive money amount—an archetypal legal remedy—to an executive tribunal and make the jury right turn on whether the target can stomach resisting until the Executive sues. Even if § 504 requires a "trial de novo" in the recovery action, § 503 authorizes the FCC to "assess" and announce a concrete forfeiture after an adjudicatory process that, in practical consequence, functions as the operative penalty determination for many regulated parties; that real-world coercion is not a mere policy concern but a foreseeable consequence of the statutory design. Meeker and Hof do not control for me because, unlike this scheme, they involved preliminary steps that were genuinely advisory and did not replicate a modern liability-and-penalty adjudication that predictably shapes behavior and outcomes before any court ever acts. I therefore cannot accept Justice Gorsuch’s proposal that enforcing "de novo means de novo" fully cures the Seventh Amendment/Article III problem where the government has already performed the core adjudicative work and attached a punitive dollar figure through the agency in the first instance.

John Roberts.reasoning: I would reverse because the Communications Act’s forfeiture scheme, as the government represents it and as the statute’s “trial de novo” recovery provision indicates, does not finally compel payment until an Article III court enters judgment, preserving any Seventh Amendment jury right at the enforcement stage. Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. permits Congress to require an initial, nonbinding administrative determination so long as the defendant can obtain a de novo judicial proceeding (including a jury where applicable) before any monetary liability is conclusively fixed. To avoid unnecessary constitutional rulings under Article III and the Seventh Amendment, I would decide narrowly that the FCC’s order has no preclusive effect and functions only as an обвинatory step triggering (not substituting for) a judicial “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture,” where liability and amount must be determined anew. Jarkesy is distinguished on the ground that it involved an agency adjudication that itself imposed binding civil penalties, whereas here the penalty is not finally imposed absent judicial recovery.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury right in “Suits at common law,” but on the government’s characterization the FCC’s forfeiture notice/order under 47 U.S.C. § 503 does not itself finally impose or collect a money judgment; the Constitution is satisfied so long as the “recovery” of any forfeiture occurs only in an Article III court in a de novo action where a jury is available for legal claims. Article III is likewise not violated when the agency’s step is nonbinding and nonpreclusive—functionally akin to a charging instrument—because the “judicial Power” to enter a binding money judgment remains vested in the courts. SEC v. Jarkesy confirms that Congress may not assign the initial adjudication of a traditional legal claim for civil penalties to an agency, but if (as petitioners represent) liability and penalty are ultimately determined anew in court without preclusive effect, this scheme fits the older line of cases permitting administrative preliminaries before full judicial trial (e.g., Meeker). On this understanding, any constitutional infirmity would arise only if FCC orders were treated as binding or given coercive legal effect prior to judicial recovery, which the statute’s de novo recovery provision is said to foreclose.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Communications Act’s text contemplates that any "suit for the recovery" of a forfeiture "imposed" proceeds as a trial de novo in an Article III court, which is the first point at which liability is conclusively adjudicated and any Seventh Amendment jury right would attach. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof, Congress may allow an agency to make an initial, nonbinding administrative determination so long as the defendant can obtain a full de novo judicial proceeding (including a jury where applicable) before any money is finally compelled. Jarkesy is distinguishable because it condemned binding administrative adjudication of civil penalties; here, on the government’s characterization accepted for purposes of this question, the FCC’s order has no preclusive effect and functions like a charging instrument rather than a final judgment. As a practical matter, invalidating the front-end administrative process would unnecessarily disrupt enforcement of complex communications regulations where Congress reasonably chose an agency screening mechanism without denying ultimate adjudication in an Article III court.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under SEC v. Jarkesy, when the Government seeks punitive civil penalties analogous to suits at common law, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial and Article III requires adjudication in an Article III court; Congress cannot evade those guarantees by placing the liability-and-penalty determination in an agency first. The FCC’s forfeiture orders, even if formally “nonbinding,” function as the Executive’s determination of legal liability and penalty amount and carry substantial coercive, real-world consequences, making the jury right contingent on nonpayment and the Government’s later choice to sue—an illusory protection in practice. Because the Communications Act authorizes the FCC to “assess” and announce large monetary forfeitures through administrative orders before any jury trial, the scheme too closely resembles the administrative penalty adjudication condemned in Jarkesy, and any later “recovery” action cannot cure the initial constitutional violation. Whatever Meeker and Hof permit, they cannot be read to allow an agency to do in substance what Jarkesy forbids: adjudicate a traditional legal claim for punitive money outside Article III and without a jury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Communications Act’s text draws a sharp line between the FCC’s administrative “impos[ition]” of a forfeiture and any judicial “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed,” and it expressly requires that recovery action to be a “trial de novo,” which makes the agency’s order non-preclusive and nonfinal for Article III and Seventh Amendment purposes. Read that way, the FCC’s forfeiture order functions like an accusation or charging instrument that authorizes litigation, while the binding adjudication of liability and the entry of a money judgment occur only in an Article III court (with a jury if the Seventh Amendment applies), avoiding the core problem identified in SEC v. Jarkesy where the agency itself finally adjudicated civil penalties. That interpretation also preserves statutory coherence and workability by allowing the FCC to investigate and plead its case administratively while keeping the ultimate coercive power—money judgment—within the judiciary. Precedents in the Meeker/Hof line support the constitutionality of administrative, nonbinding determinations that carry no preclusive effect when Congress guarantees de novo judicial proceedings for enforcement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: On the government’s representation of the Communications Act’s text that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed” proceeds as a trial de novo in an Article III court, the FCC’s notice/order functions as a nonbinding, prosecutorial step rather than a final adjudication of a traditional legal claim. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R., an administrative determination that “cuts off no defense” and “takes no question of fact from either court or jury” does not violate the Seventh Amendment, and a de novo judicial recovery action likewise satisfies Article III because the “judicial Power” to enter a binding money judgment remains with the courts. SEC v. Jarkesy controls only where the agency itself finally adjudicates liability for civil penalties in a way that displaces a jury; if the FCC’s order has no preclusive effect and compels no payment absent a fresh judicial proceeding, the constitutional problem is avoided. This conclusion depends on enforcing the statute as written: de novo means de novo, and the FCC’s order cannot be given binding or coercive legal effect in the later court action.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Communications Act’s forfeiture framework can be construed to avoid a Seventh Amendment or Article III violation because the FCC’s administrative forfeiture order does not itself compel payment and carries no preclusive effect; the government must file a “suit[] for the recovery of a forfeiture,” and the statute provides that such a suit “shall be a trial de novo” in an Article III court, where any applicable jury right may be exercised. That structure fits this Court’s longstanding approval of nonbinding, preliminary administrative determinations followed by guaranteed de novo judicial adjudication, as in Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof. SEC v. Jarkesy is distinguishable on the premise that the agency there finally adjudicated liability and penalties within the agency proceeding, whereas here the constitutionally operative adjudication of the government’s claim to money occurs only in court. Preserving that limiting construction respects precedent, history, and practical workability while avoiding the need to invalidate a longstanding regulatory enforcement scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right in “Suits at common law,” but the Communications Act’s text channels any “recovery of a forfeiture imposed” into an Article III court and, as described at argument, requires a trial de novo—meaning the FCC’s prior forfeiture order has no binding or preclusive effect in the only proceeding that can compel payment. On that understanding, the FCC’s administrative step functions as a nonfinal accusation or demand that authorizes litigation rather than an adjudication of liability, aligning with the line of cases (including Meeker and Hof) permitting nonbinding administrative determinations antecedent to full judicial trial. Jarkesy’s core holding is triggered when an agency itself finally adjudicates and imposes civil penalties for common-law-analogous claims; where Congress has instead reserved the legally operative adjudication to an Article III de novo action (with a jury if the Seventh Amendment applies), Article III and the Seventh Amendment are satisfied. Atlas Roofing’s public-rights rationale is not the decisive ground here; the dispositive point is that the statute’s enforcement mechanism vests the coercive, binding judgment in the judiciary rather than the agency.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FCC’s assessment and announcement of substantial monetary forfeitures under 47 U.S.C. § 503 functions as the government’s initial adjudication of liability for a punitive civil penalty, a quintessential “legal” remedy, and thus implicates the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right for “Suits at common law.” SEC v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. 109 (2024), emphasizes that when the government seeks civil penalties akin to common-law claims, adjudication must occur in an Article III court with a jury available, and a later “de novo” recovery/collection action does not cure a constitutional defect created by routing the liability-and-penalty determination through an agency in the first instance. Even if the government characterizes the forfeiture order as “nonbinding,” its practical coercive consequences and designed leverage over regulated parties raise Article III and procedural-fairness concerns because it effectively withdraws a traditional legal claim from judicial cognizance until after the agency has pronounced guilt and a dollar amount. Older cases like Meeker and Hof do not control where, as here, the scheme operates as a modern penalty-adjudication mechanism rather than a genuinely advisory step with no meaningful legal or practical effect.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Communications Act’s FCC forfeiture scheme unconstitutionally allows the FCC to determine and “impose” civil monetary penalties outside an Article III court and without a Seventh Amendment jury trial, notwithstanding later de novo judicial enforcement proceedings.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VII (jury trial in “Suits at common law”) and Article III (judicial power in Article III courts), as applied to the Communications Act provisions governing FCC monetary forfeitures (including the scheme for Notices of Apparent Liability/forfeiture orders and subsequent “trial de novo” recovery actions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The federal parties (FCC/United States) defend the forfeiture framework by characterizing the agency-stage determination as nonbinding—more like an indictment/complaint that authorizes a later court action—because the government still must sue in federal court to recover if the carrier refuses to pay, and that court action proceeds de novo without any preclusive effect from the Commission’s decision. On this view, there is no Seventh Amendment or Article III violation because any binding imposition of money occurs only through the Article III enforcement suit, where the defendant can obtain a jury trial; historical precedents like Meeker (and related cases such as Hof) are invoked to argue that advisory/nonfinal administrative findings that merely trigger later judicial proceedings do not themselves implicate the jury-trial right.
case_analysis.respondent_position: AT&T and Verizon argue that the scheme—especially as implemented—amounts in substance to agency adjudication of a traditional legal claim for civil penalties, which Jarkesy reaffirmed triggers the Seventh Amendment. They contend Congress cannot avoid the jury right by labeling the agency’s action “nonbinding” when it functions as a final agency determination that assesses a specific monetary forfeiture, pressures payment, and mirrors how civil-penalty regimes operate generally (i.e., most penalties can be “declined” until collection is pursued, yet they remain binding adjudications for Seventh Amendment purposes). They further argue that allowing an agency to walk up to the constitutional line—issuing what is effectively a penalty judgment that lacks formal finality only to evade a jury—raises serious Article III and unconstitutional-conditions concerns (e.g., regulated entities may feel coerced to pay or to accept collateral consequences in licensing/regulatory contexts). At minimum, they urge that FCC forfeiture orders should have no legal effect beyond a mere statement of the agency’s view and should not be given weight that effectively substitutes for an Article III judgment, and they seek relief (including return of monies paid under the challenged orders).
key_precedents: Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Comm’n (1977)
Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. (referenced in argument as resolving Seventh Amendment concerns if agency action is nonbinding)
Hof (referenced in argument; used in discussion contrasting agency findings and later judicial proceedings)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s substance-over-label point is the most serious: an FCC order that “imposes” a sum certain can look like a classic legal-penalty adjudication, and practical pressure to pay could threaten an end-run around the jury right. But the Communications Act’s enforcement mechanism—emphasized by Justice Kagan—is a recovery “suit” that “shall be a trial de novo,” and under Meeker and Capital Traction (Hof) we can and should construe that command to mean the FCC order is non-self-executing, cuts off no defenses, and has no preclusive (and no special evidentiary) effect in court, so the only legally enforceable deprivation occurs after Article III adjudication with a jury available. That narrowing construction distinguishes Jarkesy, which involved an agency’s own final, enforceable penalty judgment, and it answers Justice Sotomayor’s coercion concern at the level of law while leaving room for an as-applied challenge if collateral consequences or agency practice make the promised de novo proceeding illusory. Given our institutional role, I would decide narrowly on the statutory text and constitutional avoidance rather than facially invalidating this long-used enforcement sequence.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—that “trial de novo” means the FCC order has no preclusive or evidentiary effect—does not cure the originalist Seventh Amendment and Article III problem because Congress has still assigned the initial adjudication of a quintessential legal claim (a punitive, sum-certain forfeiture for past conduct) to an executive tribunal. Meeker and Capital Traction (Hof), as the Chief and Justice Alito invoke them, are distinguishable: there the administrative step merely supplied predicates and “cut off no defense,” whereas here the agency purports to "determine" liability and "impose" a specific monetary penalty in the first instance, which is precisely the kind of common-law analog Jarkesy treats as requiring a jury in an Article III court. Even if the later collection action is de novo, the jury right cannot depend on the Government’s discretionary choice to sue; under the Constitution’s original public meaning, the executive cannot be given what is functionally the power to render a penalty judgment and then decide whether (and when) a court will ever be involved. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on avoidance is unpersuasive here because the statutory design itself vests adjudicatory power outside Article III in a way that avoidance cannot rewrite.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to stress that the FCC’s order “imposes” a fixed punitive sum and can create real-world pressure to pay, but that practical-coercion point does not establish a facial Article III/Seventh Amendment defect when the statute’s only enforcement mechanism is the Government’s “suit for recovery” that “shall be a trial de novo.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that text is best read—consistent with Meeker and Capital Traction—to require that the FCC order cut off no defense, have no preclusive effect, and carry no binding evidentiary weight, so the only legally enforceable deprivation occurs through a fresh Article III judgment with a jury available. Jarkesy is materially different because the agency there entered a final, enforceable civil-penalty judgment in-house; here, absent judicial suit, the order is a non-self-executing demand, and any collateral-consequence or coercion-in-practice problems are better handled as as-applied challenges on an appropriate record. Under my methodology, we should adopt the narrowing construction that avoids a constitutional collision rather than treat a de novo-enforced scheme as if it were an executive money judgment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—that the FCC order has no preclusive or special evidentiary effect and that the only legally collectible deprivation occurs in a later de novo Article III suit—squarely targets the formal Meeker/Capital Traction premise that the administrative step “cuts off no defense.” But even accepting their construction, the scheme still authorizes the agency to “impose” a fixed punitive sum for past conduct in a manner that predictably secures compliance through coercive collateral consequences and regulated-party risk aversion, leaving the jury right contingent on the Government’s choice to sue at all, which Jarkesy cautions us to assess in substance rather than label. Meeker and Capital Traction are distinguishable because the administrative predicate there functioned as a noncoercive step that did not operate as the practical equivalent of a penalty judgment; here, the order’s real-world force is the point, and a de novo action that often never occurs cannot be treated as an adequate safeguard for Article III and the Seventh Amendment. For my pragmatic methodology, the constitutional injury is not cured by declaring the order “nonbinding” in court if, for many parties—especially smaller and more vulnerable ones—it effectively becomes the end of the matter without meaningful access to a jury.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s (and Justice Jackson’s) coercion-in-practice argument is the hardest: an agency-fixed punitive sum can predictably induce payment without a jury ever sitting. But textually, as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, the Act’s only legally operative mechanism to extract money is a “suit for the recovery” that “shall be a trial de novo,” so liability and amount are not legally collectible until an Article III court adjudicates anew with a jury available. To meet Justice Thomas’s substance-over-label concern and keep faith with Meeker/Capital Traction, I would adopt a narrowing construction that “trial de novo” means the FCC order has no preclusive effect and carries no binding or special evidentiary weight—i.e., it cuts off no defense—materially distinguishing Jarkesy’s in-agency final penalty judgment. The practical-pressure point may support as-applied challenges where collateral consequences make de novo review illusory, but it does not justify facial invalidation given the statute’s express de novo command and our duty to prefer a workable, constitution-avoiding construction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s substance-over-labels point—that “impose” plus practical pressure makes the FCC order function like a penalty judgment—is the hardest objection, and it rightly warns against conditioning the jury right on executive forbearance. But the enacted text controls: Congress specified that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed shall be a trial de novo,” and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that language is best read (consistent with Meeker and Capital Traction) to mean the administrative step cuts off no defense and cannot bind the court or jury in any later Article III action. On a textualist/originalist approach, we can and should adopt that narrowing construction—no preclusion and no evidentiary-binding effect—because it preserves the jury right at the only point the Government may obtain a legally enforceable money judgment, distinguishing Jarkesy’s in-agency final penalty. Justice Sotomayor’s coercion-in-practice concern may support an as-applied challenge where collateral consequences effectively negate de novo adjudication, but it does not justify facial invalidation of a scheme whose operative enforcement mechanism is a de novo court suit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s substance-over-label point is the hardest: an agency order that “imposes” a fixed punitive sum can create real pressure to pay and seems to place initial adjudication in the Executive. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively ground a saving construction in the Act’s text—any recovery “suit…shall be a trial de novo”—which, read with Meeker and Capital Traction (Hof), means the FCC order must be non-self-executing, cut off no defenses, and have no preclusive (and no special evidentiary) effect in court, so the first legally operative deprivation occurs only upon an Article III judgment with a jury available. That feature materially distinguishes Jarkesy, where the agency proceeding itself yielded a final, enforceable penalty judgment; here the agency step is best treated as an administrative assessment triggering, not supplanting, judicial adjudication. I take Justice Sotomayor’s practical-coercion concern seriously, but under an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach it supports an as-applied challenge if collateral consequences or agency practice negate genuine de novo review, not facial invalidation of a scheme that—properly construed—preserves the jury right in the only enforceable collection action.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s practical-coercion critique is the hardest, because a large, agency-set sum can predictably induce payment without any jury ever convening. But under the Communications Act’s text, the only legally operative mechanism to extract money is a “suit for the recovery” that “shall be a trial de novo,” and—consistent with the Chief Justice’s reliance on Meeker and Capital Traction—that means the FCC order must cut off no defenses and bind neither judge nor jury. Justice Thomas is right that “impose” can sound adjudicative, yet read in statutory context it functions as an administrative assessment that triggers (rather than consummates) the Article III proceeding where the government must prove liability and amount anew. To the extent coercion stems from collateral consequences or agency practice, Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction (no preclusion and no special evidentiary weight) answers the facial Article III/Seventh Amendment objection while preserving room for an as-applied challenge on a developed record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—that “trial de novo” bars preclusion and denies the FCC order any special evidentiary weight—meaningfully improves the scheme at the back end, but it still does not cure the front-end procedural defect that Justice Sotomayor highlights: the agency’s order fixes a punitive sum in a way that predictably induces payment without any Article III jury ever being convened. Meeker and Capital Traction are not decisive for me because their administrative predicates did not operate as a concrete penalty assessment with the same practical coercion and collateral consequences; here, the Government can obtain compliance without ever filing the de novo suit that supposedly safeguards the jury right. And Jarkesy’s substance-over-label principle, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, is implicated when Congress assigns initial adjudication of a classic legal penalty to the Executive and makes the jury right contingent on the Government’s later litigation choice. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the statutory promise of de novo review is too often illusory in practice to accept this arrangement on its face as consistent with the Seventh Amendment.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Communications Act’s forfeiture mechanism can be sustained on narrow grounds because the FCC’s Notice of Apparent Liability/forfeiture order is not self-executing: if the carrier refuses to pay, the United States must bring a "trial de novo" recovery action in an Article III court, where the defendant may demand a Seventh Amendment jury. Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof support the proposition that nonbinding administrative findings that merely trigger later de novo judicial proceedings do not themselves infringe the jury-trial right, and the statutory command of de novo recovery mitigates Article III concerns by reserving the binding money judgment to the court. SEC v. Jarkesy is distinguishable because it involved an agency proceeding that itself adjudicated liability and imposed enforceable civil penalties, whereas here the operative legal imposition occurs only upon judicial enforcement. Preserving this reading also respects longstanding administrative practice while avoiding a broad constitutional ruling that would unsettle similar federal schemes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right in “Suits at common law,” and a government demand for a fixed civil monetary penalty is the kind of legal claim historically tried to a jury; Jarkesy confirms that Congress may not repackage such penalty adjudications as administrative proceedings to evade that guarantee. Although the Communications Act contemplates a later “trial de novo” in a judicial “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed,” the statute’s text authorizes the FCC itself to determine and “impose” the forfeiture in the first instance—an exercise of judicial power outside Article III when it functions, in substance, as a penalty judgment. Meeker does not save the scheme because it addressed non-common-law regulatory action and merely allowed a rebuttable presumption that “cuts off no defense” and “takes no question of fact from either court or jury,” whereas FCC forfeiture orders here operate as an agency adjudication of a traditional legal claim and place constitutionally significant pressure on regulated parties to pay without a jury. The Constitution’s original public meaning does not permit Congress to condition the availability of a jury on the government’s discretionary choice to file a later collection action.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Textually, the Communications Act contemplates that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed shall be a trial de novo,” which indicates that the legally operative imposition of monetary liability occurs, if at all, through an Article III enforcement action rather than conclusively at the Commission stage. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co., Congress may authorize nonbinding administrative findings that merely trigger later judicial proceedings so long as the subsequent Article III court adjudicates the facts and law de novo, preserving the Seventh Amendment jury right in that enforcement suit. Jarkesy is distinguishable because it involved the SEC finally adjudicating and entering binding civil penalties within the agency itself, whereas the FCC’s forfeiture order here lacks preclusive effect and cannot be collected without a new de novo court action. Practically, invalidating this scheme would disrupt longstanding civil-penalty enforcement structures and impair effective regulatory enforcement without a clear constitutional necessity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Communications Act’s forfeiture process, as implemented, looks like an agency adjudication of a classic suit at common law for money penalties, which under the Seventh Amendment must be resolved in an Article III court with a jury unless it fits a genuine “public rights” exception. SEC v. Jarkesy confirms that civil-penalty actions mirroring traditional legal claims trigger the jury-trial right, and Congress cannot evade that guarantee by labeling the FCC’s forfeiture order “nonbinding” when it assesses a definite sum and predictably pressures payment through practical and regulatory consequences. Meeker and Capital Traction v. Hof do not save this scheme if the agency’s determination functions as more than a purely advisory finding with no legal or coercive effect; a “trial de novo” later is not an adequate preservation of the right when the government can effectively obtain compliance without ever bringing the Article III collection suit. Because the scheme empowers the FCC to determine and effectively impose civil penalties outside Article III, it raises serious Article III and Seventh Amendment concerns that require treating such forfeiture orders as constitutionally infirm (or at minimum stripping them of operative effect until an Article III adjudication).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Communications Act’s text provides that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed” “shall be a trial de novo,” which is best read to mean the FCC’s forfeiture order does not itself finally impose a legally collectible money judgment; the binding imposition occurs only in the subsequent Article III action where a jury may be demanded. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof, Congress may permit nonbinding administrative determinations that carry no preclusive effect and merely trigger a later de novo judicial proceeding without violating the Seventh Amendment or Article III. Jarkesy is therefore distinguishable because it involved the agency itself entering a final, enforceable civil-penalty adjudication rather than an administrative step antecedent to de novo court enforcement. To avoid constitutional edge-cases, I would also construe the scheme to give FCC forfeiture orders no collateral estoppel or evidentiary weight in the enforcement suit beyond what ordinary non-preclusive governmental allegations would carry.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Communications Act provides that any “suit for the recovery of a forfeiture imposed” shall be a “trial de novo,” and that text is best read to mean the FCC’s notice/forfeiture order is not itself a conclusive money judgment but a preliminary executive determination that must be proved anew in an Article III court. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof, Congress may allow nonbinding administrative findings that merely trigger a later, independent judicial proceeding where the defendant can demand a jury, without violating Article III or the Seventh Amendment. Jarkesy confirms that binding agency adjudication of traditional legal penalties requires a jury, but it does not control where the agency action has no preclusive effect and the government must obtain any enforceable monetary judgment in court. If, in practice, FCC orders were given binding or preclusive effect or used to extract payment without meaningful access to de novo judicial adjudication, that would raise serious constitutional concerns, but on the statutory scheme as written the ultimate imposition occurs in the Article III recovery suit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Communications Act’s forfeiture scheme can be construed to avoid a Seventh Amendment or Article III violation because the FCC’s “imposition” of a forfeiture is not legally binding in the constitutional sense: if the carrier declines to pay, the United States must bring a “trial de novo” recovery action in an Article III court, where the defendant may demand a jury on the civil-penalty claim. That structure fits within Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co. and Capital Traction Co. v. Hof, which allow nonfinal administrative determinations that merely trigger a later de novo judicial proceeding without displacing the jury’s factfinding role. SEC v. Jarkesy confirms that when the Government seeks civil penalties akin to common-law suits, the Seventh Amendment jury right applies—but here it is satisfied in the subsequent Article III enforcement suit, and the agency’s order should carry no preclusive effect. Given the statutory promise of de novo adjudication and the workability/legitimacy costs of invalidating longstanding administrative frameworks, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit and uphold the scheme as properly construed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, the Communications Act distinguishes between a forfeiture "imposed" by the Commission and a subsequent "suit for the recovery" that "shall be a trial de novo," indicating Congress contemplated that any legally binding extraction of money occurs only through an Article III enforcement action. Under Meeker v. Lehigh Valley R.R. Co., Congress may permit an agency’s non-preclusive, nonbinding findings to precede a de novo judicial proceeding without infringing the Seventh Amendment because the administrative step "cuts off no defense" and takes no fact question from the court or jury. Jarkesy controls when the agency itself finally adjudicates and imposes a civil penalty; but where the government must still prove liability and amount anew in federal court, with no preclusive effect from the agency order, the Seventh Amendment and Article III concerns are materially mitigated. To the extent respondents argue practical coercion, that contention goes more to policy and implementation than to the scheme’s constitutional validity given the preserved de novo Article III adjudication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Communications Act’s forfeiture scheme, as structured and implemented, authorizes the FCC to adjudicate and announce a fixed, punitive monetary forfeiture in a manner that functions like a legal liability determination for civil penalties—an archetypal “Suit[] at common law” that, under the Seventh Amendment and Jarkesy, must be tried to a jury in an Article III court. The government’s reliance on later “trial de novo” collection actions does not cure the constitutional problem where the agency’s forfeiture order operates in practice as a coercive, final penalty assessment that pressures payment and can trigger collateral regulatory consequences, raising serious Article III concerns about agencies exercising core judicial power. Meeker and Capital Traction (Hof) do not control because they involved genuinely nonbinding administrative findings that merely informed or triggered subsequent judicial proceedings, whereas here the statute and agency practice treat the forfeiture as “imposed” prior to any Article III adjudication, even if collection requires a later suit. Given the practical consequences for regulated parties and the constitutional baseline that punitive monetary penalties for past conduct resemble traditional legal claims, procedural fairness requires jury-triable adjudication in court rather than an agency-first penalty judgment.
